summary: Defines an IMAP4 extension for administrative limits on resource usage, called quotas, to be viewed and changed through the IMAP protocol. It was replaced by RFC 9208.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2087 adds IMAP commands for setting mailbox resource limits and checking how much of each resource is used. It groups limits into named quota roots that can apply to one or more mailboxes; RFC 9208 later replaced this specification.

questions: how to check mailbox quota over imap
what are quota roots in imap
what is an imap quota root
how do imap quota commands work
what does the imap storage resource measure
subtitle: An IMAP extension for reporting and managing mailbox resource limits.

tldr.problem: IMAP clients need a standard way to learn which resource limits apply to mailboxes and how much of each resource is used.
tldr.mechanism: The QUOTA extension defines commands to set and retrieve limits and responses that report quota roots, resource usage, and limits.

sections.title: Quota Roots and Resources
sections.content:
An IMAP server supports this extension when it reports the QUOTA capability. It can apply limits to resources, each identified by a name with an implementation-defined meaning. The RFC gives STORAGE, measured as the sum of message sizes in units of 1024 octets, and MESSAGE, the number of messages, as examples.

Each mailbox can have zero or more named quota roots. Mailboxes that share a quota root also share its resource limits. Quota root names do not have to match mailbox names.
sections.plainLanguage: A quota root is a named set of resource limits. Several mailboxes can share one quota root, and resource names describe what the server measures.

sections.title: Commands for Quotas
sections.content:
SETQUOTA replaces the resource limits for a named quota root with the supplied list. A server may create a root that did not exist before. GETQUOTA asks for the usage and limits of one root. GETQUOTAROOT asks which roots apply to a mailbox and returns usage and limits for each.

The server reports each quota as a QUOTA response containing the resource name, current usage, and limit. Resources not listed are unlimited; an empty resource list means that the root has no administrative limits.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can set limits, check one quota root, or ask which quota roots apply to a mailbox. The server reports usage and limits for each listed resource.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content: The RFC warns that resource use by other users may be confidential. Implementations should ensure that quota commands do not violate the site's security policy and should not reveal other users' usage to people who are not authorized.
sections.plainLanguage: Quota information can reveal how much other users store. Servers should protect it from unauthorized users.

references.text: Crispin, M., "Internet Message Access Protocol - Version 4", RFC 1730, December 1994.
